Chapter 2: The Hidden Costs of Approval-Seeking and Suppressed Needs
Now that we’ve shed some light on the ‘Nice Guy’ pattern, let’s take a closer look at what it actually costs us in real life.
You might think that trying to keep everyone happy creates harmony and brings people closer. But in reality, it can do just the opposite—leaving you with strained relationships, unmet needs, and that lingering sense of dissatisfaction you just can’t shake.
One of the biggest costs? It’s the slow, steady erosion of your self-respect. When you keep putting your own needs and boundaries on the back burner just to please others, you’re sending a message—not just to everyone around you, but to yourself—that your feelings and desires don’t really matter. Over time, this takes a toll. Before you know it, your self-worth starts slipping, and you can’t help but feel like people are taking you for granted.
And when it comes to relationships, always hiding what you really think or feel doesn’t bring you closer—it actually pushes people away. Intimacy, real closeness, is built on honesty and vulnerability. But if you’re always agreeable, or you bite your tongue instead of speaking up, it’s tough to make a genuine connection. Partners can usually feel that something’s missing, even if they can’t put their finger on what it is. The relationship might seem calm on the surface, but deep down, it’s missing the real depth that comes from sharing openly.
Now, let’s talk about work. If you find it hard to set boundaries or stand up for yourself, you might end up overloaded, missing out on good opportunities, or feeling invisible. The people you work with might start expecting you to always say “yes,” making it even harder to draw the line or ask for what you need. This can quickly lead to burnout, resentment, and that nagging feeling of being undervalued.
But it doesn’t stop there. The emotional cost of bottling up your needs and desires is huge. If you keep frustration, disappointment, or anger locked inside, those feelings don’t just disappear. Instead, they tend to sneak out in all sorts of unhealthy ways—like being passive-aggressive, snapping unexpectedly, or just withdrawing from people altogether. The longer you ignore these emotions, the more they chip away at your happiness and your connections with others.
Here’s something that happens a lot: covert contracts. These are the unspoken deals you make in your head—like, “If I go out of my way to help, I’ll get love or appreciation in return.” But the thing is, nobody else knows about these deals except you. So when your expectations aren’t met, disappointment and resentment start piling up—often without the other person even realizing what was expected of them.
Think about this: maybe you help a friend move, secretly hoping they’ll be there for you during a rough patch. But if your friend doesn’t step up, you end up feeling hurt or even angry—even though you never actually told them what you needed. This “giving with strings attached” creates confusion and tension, and it’s a recipe for frustration in any relationship.
So, what are the real costs of falling into the ‘Nice Guy’ pattern? Let’s break it down:
Loss of self-respect and personal identity.
Relationships that stay on the surface, missing real intimacy.
Chronic resentment and frustration that just won’t go away.
Feeling stuck or burned out at work because your boundaries keep getting crossed.
Emotional ups and downs, or simply pulling away from people.
And, maybe most of all, needs and expectations that never get voiced or met.
Seeing these hidden costs is a powerful motivator for change. It becomes clear that chasing approval and dodging conflict doesn’t just fall short—it actually makes things worse.
The next step? Start challenging those old beliefs and fears that keep the pattern going. Try out new ways of relating, both to yourself and to everyone around you. That’s how real growth begins.
